pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Lakers: Austin Reaves pulls a Doncic to beat Detroit
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 8: Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket during the game against the Detroit Pistons on November 8, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Sevald/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Who needs Luka Doncic when you have the US equivalent from Newark, Arkansas, Austin Reaves? The Los Angeles Lakers guard scored a game-high 43 as his MVP-level teammate rested with a back injury, propelling LA past the Detroit Pistons 121-116.

Honestly, the game had no reason to be as close as it was in the end. The Lakers led 40-14 one basket into the second quarter courtesy of insane shotmaking (hitting 72% from the floor) and an insane amount of Pistons miscues, including having more turnovers (eight) than made baskets (six).

But the Pistons, being the Pistons, weren’t about to give up. While Detroit pulled within one point early in the fourth quarter, the Lakers led wire to wire. So while it was only marginally competitive from Detroit’s point of view, it was certainly an instructive game. Here are some of the things I learned:

1. Kevin Huerter

Kevin Huerter is going to be a critical component of the Pistons’ rotation this season. In a game where Detroit’s entire backcourt didn’t really show up to play (both Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson were largely no-shows until some fourth-quarter scoring), Huerter was by far the biggest bright spot for the Pistons.

It also happened to be his best game in a Detroit uniform. Huerter hit four three-pointers, scored 24 points overall, and added five rebounds, five assists, five blocks(?!) and two steals. Ever since the Pistons traded for him at the deadline last season, it was clear Huerter makes winning plays, and you were hoping he’d be able to combine that with rediscovering his 3-point shooting stroke from earlier in his career. The early returns indicate the shot might be back, as well as everything that goes with it. After tonight, he’s hitting 40% from deep this season.

2. John Collins and Paul Reed

Detroit’s starting front court simply does not work, and it will never work. For as long as Jalen Duren remains sidelined or off the floor this season, this is going to be a significant issue for the Pistons. Duren is ramping back up from a hamstring injury and will be out two more weeks. Detroit has been, and will continue to be able to weather that storm. But it ain’t pretty, and any additional time off from Duren will have me significantly worried.

Most will want to pin the blame on the newcomer John Collins, and he has certainly played worse than Reed, but I think it’s the combination that brings out the worst in both players. Each is the kind of big man that relies on the gravity from teammates that allows them to use their athleticism to create the chaos that makes them effective. With both of them on the floor, it’s two bouncy balls pinging around the floor with no semblance of a plan on how to actually get the ball to the rim. The defense is also bad, and the rebounding is even worse. It’s an ugly situation, and it was exacerbated tonight by both men getting out-physicaled by the behemoth seven-footer Walker Kessler. Kessler, the Lakers’ big offseason addition, had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including seven on the offensive end. The Lakers also dominated the Pistons in the paint, 58-46.

Again, the lion’s share of the blame goes to Collins. He’s been quite bad all season, and it’s getting less clear by the day how he’s going to turn it around and be a positive force for the Pistons. I don’t think he’s ever met a 50-50 ball he couldn’t surrender to the opposition. But the pathway to him playing well lies with sharing the floor with Duren. Get well soon, JD.

3. Austin Reaves

The Pistons were correct in trying to give Austin Reaves the bag this offseason. Detroit reportedly was ready to give the wing a max contract this offseason as the second scorer and potential missing piece in a Detroit Pistons title run. Once the Lakers believed the pending RFA had a max offer on the table, they quickly moved to get an agreement to sign him on the eve of free agency so he’d never hit the market.

Reaves was insane tonight. The degree of difficulty on his shots begged belief. He was able to create space, get balanced, and score at all three levels. It was a sight to behold, and he was by far the best player on the floor for either team tonight.

4. Daniss Jenkins

Daniss has that dog in him, especially under two scenarios: 1. There is an impending buzzer. 2. He feels like his team is getting punked. Jenkins was truly the other hero of the game behind Huerter. He hit yet another buzzer-beater tonight, and he scored a career-high 31 points. When the Pistons were down huge, Jenkins got that look in his eye, as if to say, “This is not going to happen.”

From there, Jenkins started firing away from deep, and he was hitting. In the end, he canned eight three-pointers. He was also the ONLY Pistons player to go to the free-throw line more than once in the game. Really, Jenkins is like a better version of Marcus Sasser. He’s got scoring in his blood, and he’s more of an off-guard than a point guard, despite being stuck in a point guard’s body. He’s got three inches on Sasser and better floor vision, so he’s better overall and can cosplay as a point guard better than Sass, but Jenkins works best in this Pistons lineup when he’s not running the offense.

4. The refs.

The referees love the Lakers. Nothing else needs to be said.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs Lakers preview: Best Defense vs best offense
pistons.body:
Does it get any better than the No. 1 offense versus the No. 1 defense? The Detroit Pistons find themselves in that matchup as the 122-point-per-game Los Angeles Lakers visit Motown tonight.

Luka Dončić and the Lakers put up plenty of buckets, but scoring on Detroit is still an impossible task. The Pistons only surrender 101 points a game. Smothering defense every night.

Detroit’s defense has its biggest test of the season if Dončić suits up this evening. He’s questionable with lower back tightness.

It would be a shame if we’re robbed of Cade Cunningham going head-to-head with another MVP candidate. The bigger shame would be if we miss out on Dončić versus Ausar Thompson. That matchup is like Jerry Rice versus Deion Sanders with how both are operating.

GAME VITALS

Where: Little Caesars Arena, Detroit, MI

When: 6 PM EST

Watch: TV20 Detroit/DAZN-DET

Odds: Pistons (-4.5)

Analysis

Detroit hasn’t played since Wednesday’s loss to the Philadelphia 76ers. They’ve had plenty of time to rest up. They’ll need it if Dončić suits up.

Dončić is averaging 40 points. He’s shooting 42% on nearly 14 3s a game. He gets to the line more than anybody. It’s basically no stopping Dončić at the moment. This is a Wilt Chamberlain-like hot streak. Those two are the only players to average 40 nine games into the season. Whew, to say he’s balling is an understatement.

But tasks like this are why the Pistons employ Ausar Thompson. If *anybody* can slow Dončić down, it’s the best perimeter defender on the planet. Dončić usually has success against quick defenders with wiry strength, but Ausar is bigger and stronger this season. We’ll be keeping tabs on how Ausar takes Dončić’s bumps tonight. Ausar has the quick hands to disrupt things as well.

This might be a game where we see Paul Reed getting to the level and blitzing a bunch. J.B. Bickerstaff may decide to get the ball out of Dončić’s hands and force someone else to beat them. Reed is capable of coming to the level on screens and muddying things up.

I’m sure Dončić will see some Cade tonight too. Cade won’t make it easy with his sturdy frame. On the other end, the Lakers only have a few perimeter defenders to throw at Cade.

Matisse Thybulle is firmly in LA’s rotation as he’s started all 10 games. He’s still a defensive playmaking threat. Cade deals with defenders like this nightly, but Thybulle is a plus defender nonetheless. So is Ziaire Williams. The springy 25-year-old treats every possession as if he’ll never get in the game again if he doesn’t go hard.

Those two are solid defensively, and Jake LaRavia competes. Outside of that, Detroit will have plenty of favorable matchups (Walker Kessler is a great rim protector and is off to a good offensive start. He can make a difference).

Dončić displays effort and is trying to shake the terrible defender narrative on his name, but attacking him is still the best way to slow him down. Make him work and keep him involved in actions.

Austin Reaves falls into the same boat. He’s under Dončić on the Lakers’ best defenders on the team list. Anybody with that matchup should look to be aggressive.

Reaves spends most of his time covering shooting guards. Will JJ Redick make Reaves chase Duncan Robinson all night? That’s probably not ideal. Robinson runs even great defenders into the ground.

Robinson’s light-em-up stretch continues as he’s fourth in 3s made (35). Only Dončić, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, and Steph Curry have made more.

Detroit is letting it fly from deep as a team. According to Cleaning the Glass, 40 percent of their shots are coming from 3 (15th) compared to 31 percent last year (29th). Their rim rate has flipped the other way, but getting Jalen Duren back should rectify that.

The best offense versus the best defense is a mandatory viewing appointment. Can Ausar slow down the MVP-favorite? Do the Pistons show why they’re an elite defense and smother Dončić as a team? Does Cade deliver a masterclass against a guy he’ll be compared to for the foreseeable future if he’s in the MVP race? We’ll find out at 6 PM. Be there!

Projected starting lineup

Detroit Pistons (6-2): Cade Cunningham, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins, Paul Reed

Los Angeles Lakers (8-2): Luka Dončić, Austin Reaves, Matisse Thybulle, Jake LaRavia, Walker Kessler

Question of the day

What are your thoughts on Austin Reaves? He reportedly did not want to be drafted by Detroit. Does that still bother you?

pistons.headline: The Pistons go from owning to getting owned in the paint
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Jalen Duren #0 of the Detroit Pistons looks on from the bench during a game against the Philadelphia 76ers at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

During a tumultuous playoff run and a prolonged offseason contract negotiation, Detroit Pistons fans were ready to say goodbye to Jalen Duren. Well, Duren has been out for six of eight games, and it turns out that Duren is the most indispensable member of the Pistons aside from Cade Cunningham.

A hamstring strain has knocked Duren out for six straight and counting, and boy, do you feel that every moment of every Pistons game.

Pundits and fans alike had easy diagnoses for what ailed the 60-win team during a disappointing second-round exit last season. Detroit needed a second scorer and much more perimeter shooting to succeed in the postseason. Its second-best player, the All-NBA big man Duren, couldn’t effectively operate in a congested, constipated offense when opponents had so much extra time to prepare their defense. That had a trickle-down effect on Cade Cunningham and on offensively limited players the Pistons relied on, like Ausar Thompson, Javonte Green, and Ron Holland.

This offseason, the Pistons seemingly tried and failed to add their second scorer (a planned run at Austin Reaves fizzled, and trade interest in players such as Kyrie Irving and Kevin Durant went nowhere). But they certainly addressed the team’s lack of perimeter punch. Detroit added guys such as Isaiah Joe, John Collins, and Taurean Prince. They re-signed midseason acquisition Kevin Huerter. They reformulated their offensive game plan to create more movement, space, and offensive responsibility among their non-Cade players. So far this season, the perimeter offense has hummed. Detroit is a top-10 team in 3-point shooting and almost middle of the pack in attempts despite Isaiah Joe missing most of the season to injury.

Detroit is 6-2, losing to the New York Knicks and on Wednesday night to the East-leading Philadelphia 76ers. Calls after both games from fans and casual watchers immediately turn to the team’s lack of that second star as the biggest issue. While that still might be a deal-breaker in the players, I would argue that the actual biggest issue in the season’s first eight games is Detroit’s collapse in its former ability to absolutely own the paint.

In other words, it’s not the lack of a Kyrie or a Durant or a Devin Booker. It’s the lack of Duren.

Last season, Detroit led the NBA in points in the paint, mostly behind Duren’s elite rim gravity and chemistry with Cade Cunningham and Detroit’s other ball handlers. Last season, the Pistons led the NBA with 57.9 points in the paint and were fourth in opponents’ paint scoring. They had a scoring differential inside of 14.2 points per game.  This season, Detroit ranks just 22nd in the paint at 44.8, down 13.1 points per game.

Rim gravity, it turns out, is just as important as perimeter shooting in creating the space needed to run a successful offense.

Paul Reed is a dynamic scorer inside, and he has some pop to his game. But he isn’t a rim runner like Duren. You give it to him on the block, and you let him work his magic. John Collins is opportunistic in transition, but those opportunities are dried up when he is the only big on the floor applying rim pressure, usually trying to duck in from the corners.

Ausar has the ball in his hands more, and it is working to create opportunities from others on the perimeter, but it is taking away a lot of those dunker-spot opportunities and back cuts that Thompson feasted on last season.

The lack of inside pressure is manifesting in other ways. Detroit has gone from a top-5 team in second-chance points to 22nd. They are 28th in offensive rebounding. Last season, they were third.

This team needs Jalen Duren back ASAP. And I think fans need to start reckoning with how crucial he is for this team to succeed.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs 76ers final score: Detroit falls short in East battle
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons drives around Vj Edgecombe #77 of the Philadelphia 76ers during the first half at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Pistons (6-2) fall short in the battle between the top teams in the Eastern Conference. The Philadelphia 76ers (8-1) outlasted Detroit 112-106. Philly got up by as many as 18 points, but Detroit never truly went away. The 76ers’ stardom showed its head tonight.

After holding Jaylen Brown to 16 points in the first meeting of the season, he surpassed that in the first half this time around. Brown poured in 30 points for the game while converting on 11 of his 19 shots. He rained in spot-up 3s, as it was tough to stick with him with the way Philly forced Detroit into scramble mode throughout the ballgame. Brown had a clutch block on Cade, and his presence was felt on both sides of the ball.

This is not 2023 Joel Embiid, but he’s still a force. Embiid still draws double teams and can get any big in foul trouble. He and Tolu Smith got into a dust-up that injected some life into Detroit, but Philly found a way to withstand every Detroit storm.

Duncan Robinson went on a few personal runs that seemed to turn the tide in Detroit’s favor. The sharpshooter went for 27 points and buried an unconscious seven triples. Robinson’s ability to look past the hands in his face to shoot the rock will pay dividends all season. It didn’t work out tonight, but Robinson is off to a different type of start as a sniper.

Cade Cunningham tried to put on his cape and emptied the clip. He couldn’t find it from deep but got good looks. He went for 26 points, 11 assists, and seven boards. He got to the charity stripe and nailed every attempt (7-7). Cade had another LeBron-like chasedown block — this time in LeBron’s presence.

At this point, those are truly Cade-like chasedowns, and Brown’s missed layup here shows Cade’s reputation as a chasedown artist is evident.

Jaylen Brown misses the wide open layup. 😬 pic.twitter.com/jMyfS41RJG
— Hoop Central (@TheHoopCentral) November 5, 2026

VJ Edgecombe had a fast break sequence where he u-turned it because Cade was on the hunt again. Special defender.

Ausar Thompson’s special stuff came on the boards as he snagged 17 rebounds tonight. From the opening possession, he was pogo-sticking down low to help Paul Reed and John Collins in the paint. AT chipped in 11 points, and his shot from the line continues to look better. He was 3-for-4 tonight; you’ll take the small improvements wherever you can.

John Collins had his best offensive game in a few games. He was getting behind the defense, throwing down head-top slams. His ability to be a paint finisher and hit threes is why he’s here. He only shot one 3 tonight. The Pistons need more.

Collins should look better when Duren comes back, in theory. Duren has rim-gravity that forces defenses to account for one of the best finishers in basketball. This was the first game where I thought Detroit missed Duren badly. From a talent perspective, Detroit was outgunned tonight.

LeBron James controlled the tempo in spurts of the game. He was playing like that OG at the Y who’s keeping up with the youngins on pure know-how. LeBron draws two to the ball, Embiid does, Brown does, and Tyrese Maxey does. There’s a lot of star power over there, and this is a team Detroit could see in the long run.

The Pistons did not have their sharpest defensive night, and Philly still only cracked 112. It was just one of the games. Detroit shifts their focus to another superstar in Luka Dončić. He and the Los Angeles Lakers travel to Detroit on Sunday as the Pistons take on their first Western Conference team of the season.

One benefit in Detroit’s favor is that this is a nationally televised game on ESPN, and it seems like Cade Cunningham loves to come up big when the lights are brightest for national television. pistons.headline: Pistons vs 76ers preview:  East’s top two teams square off on National TV
pistons.body:
If you are to believe preseason predictions, this game being a showdown between the East’s top two teams could come as a bit of a surprise.  Pistons fans knew this team would be good, but many talking heads predicted a falloff this season while everybody was on board with the 76ers being one of the best teams in the league.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that the team that was 1st in the East last season is once again competing for the top seed in the East, but talking heads have to make their money somehow.  ESPN at least had the foresight to pickup this game and you get what should be a very fun early-season showdown between two teams that have only lost one game each.

The 76ers and Pistons have played once this season and the Pistons won, but it is tough to draw any conclusions since both teams were missing a couple of starters.

Game Vitals

Where:  Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, MI
When:  Wednesday, November 4 at 7 pm EST
Watch:  ESPN
Odds:  Detroit (-2.5)

Analysis

The Pistons will be without Jalen Duren and Isaiah Joe, who was already ruled out for this game last night.  The Pistons were missing Jalen Duren in the last matchup between these teams and also Ausar Thompson, who they will have back.  But, Isaiah Joe did suffer the hip injury that is still keeping him out during the 1st quarter of the last matchup, so the Pistons are trading one injured player for another.

With this being a National TV game and the 76ers getting a day of rest, I would suspect that everybody plays for them tonight.  In the last matchup, the 76ers did not have Joel Embiid or VJ Edgecombe, which really put their lack of depth to the test.

Joel Embiid’s size and ability on the glass could become a problem for the Pistons, who will continue to start the undersized Paul Reed and likely use John Collins to back him up.  Without Jalen Duren, rebounding was already going to be a problem, but the Pistons have been able to overcome it during his absence.

In the last matchup, the Pistons were able to contain Tyrese Maxey through 3 quarters before he started hitting shots in the 4th.  It was a bit of shocking development since the Pistons were without Ausar Thompson, but without some of the other stars for the 76ers, they could focus their defense more on stopping Maxey.  The 76ers have a lot of star power, but their biggest offensive threat is arguably Maxey, who can hit shots from anywhere on the court and can use his quickness with the ball to get to where he wants.  I would expect Ausar Thompson to draw the Tyrese Maxey matchup which will allow Cade Cunningham to guard Jaylen Brown since he has the size to keep up with him.

I am not really sure what the Pistons are going to do about the Joel Embiid matchup.  Paul Reed is outsized by him and also can have some issues with fouling and Joel Embiid has made a living off of bating fouls throughout his career.  Paul Reed is going to have to stay disciplined, as I don’t think the Pistons can afford to have heavy minutes of John Collins at center or Tolu Smith.  I have full confidence in the Pistons’ ability to matchup with the rest of the 76ers starting lineup, but the most concern I have is this matchup and it very well could swing the game.

If there is one certainty for the Pistons, it is that Cade Cunningham is difficult to slow down, especially with how he is playing now.  He is coming off a 33 points masterclass against the Charlotte Hornets on Monday in only 27 minutes where he absolutely took over the game and turned a single-digit lead into a 20-plus point blowout.  Cade Cunningham always starts off the season slow, but he seems to be hitting his stride now.  His 3-ball is consistently falling as he is shooting 37% from beyond the arc, which is a significant development for his offensive creation abilities and efficiency.

He is going to have to put together another masterclass if the Pistons want any hope to win this game.  During Jalen Duren’s absence, the Pistons have been able to win games through their high-level defense, but their offense has left a lot to be desired.  With Isaiah Joe out and Duncan Robinson going through a bit of a cold stretch, the Pistons shooting fell off a bit and they went four games in a row scoring 110 points or less.

However, everything seemed to get back on track on Monday against the Hornets, so hopefully that continues.

One player the Pistons are hoping gets back on track is John Collins.  He had his best game as a Piston in the last game against the 76ers and has proceeded to score single-digit points in every game since then.  With Jalen Duren out, he has had to play a lot more center than he was probably planning on playing, but he has also had difficulties finding a consistent offensive role.  Another big John Collins game would be a huge help in this matchup

The Joel Embiid matchup concerns me with the Pistons lack of frontcourt size, but if they can defend Tyrese Maxey like they did in the last matchup, they have a shot to takedown the 76ers and claim the top seed in the Eastern Conference.

lions.headline: 11 winners, 8 losers from Detroit Lions’ win over the Miami Dolphins
lions.body:
MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 08: Alim McNeill #54 of the Detroit Lions pressures Malik Willis #2 of the Miami Dolphins during the fourth quarter of the game at Hard Rock Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images

It had been an emotional week for the Detroit Lions. A week after losing Jack Campbell, one of the heartbeats of the team, to a serious injury, Detroit not only had to weather his absence on the field but off it as well.

It was far from Detroit’s best game, but they will leave Miami with a win. The Dolphins did an admirable job silencing the Lions offense, but their own offensive deficiencies did little to threaten the Lions defense. That resulted in a game with a fair number of field goals, punts, and even a fake punt from each team. Detroit was the only team to find the end zone, but that was all it took to close out this game.

Which players emerged from this tilt as a winner or loser?

Winner: Aidan Hutchinson, DE

If NFL officiating was consistent and accurate, Hutchinson might have set an NFL record for holding penalties drawn in a game. The Lions’ star pass rusher was a menace on Sunday, bringing more heat than Miami’s basketball team. He ended the game with just two tackles and a quarterback hit, but that does not tell the whole story. On every drive and nearly every snap, Hutchinson was bullying his opposition, whether it was right tackle Austin Jackson, left tackle Patrick Paul, or whoever was unfortunate enough to line up across from him.

Officially, Hutchinson drew two holding penalties (one on Jackson, one on tight end Will Kacmarek), but there were at least a half dozen uncalled holds. The most egregious one came late in the second quarter, as Jackson essentially horse-collar tackled Hutchinson. The Dolphins wound up missing their end-of-half field goal attempt, so that was karmic retribution.

Hutchinson is a consistent contributor on defense, but he has the occasional game where he goes supernova. This was one of those outings.

Losers: Tate Ratledge, Miles Frazier, Blake Miller, Christian Mahogany, Hank Fraley, OL

Jared Goff was in hell against the Dolphins pass rush, and the performance of these three players was a large reason why. The right side of the offensive line was under siege all day long. Ratledge allowed a sack on the second offensive drive, forcing a punt. Miller fought a losing battle against Chop Robinson out at right tackle. Though Miller was not credited with a sack allowed, he was responsible for the hit on Goff that led to his interception—on that same play, Ratledge was bulldozed by Zach Sieler. Miller was also flagged for a hold halfway through the fourth quarter.

The shock of the day was the benching of Christian Mahogany for Frazier at left guard. Mahogany had been playing at a high level next to Penei Sewell across six games, yet the Lions coaching staff made him ride the pine against Miami. Frazier gave up a sack on the first drive, then committed a holding penalty on the third drive. Later in the second half, Frazier got blown up on a rushing play, leading to a 3-yard loss. In the third quarter, another immediate pressure from Frazier forced a rushed throw and resulted in yet another field goal.

Frazier was struggling immensely against the Dolphins, yet the Lions did not substitute Mahogany back into the lineup. The benching was disciplinary in nature, per Dan Campbell, so Mahogany certainly deserves blame, yet at a certain point, you are trying to win football games—benching one of your best linemen for an entire game is a massive risk, even if it sends a message. Not only does the offense suffer, but you also subject Jared Goff to multiple hits. However, you have to trust that the team made this decision knowing the consequences. That ultimately reflects poorly on Mahogany. He was not in the locker room when the media arrived to further explain what happened.

A lot of these offensive line’s struggles fall on offensive line coach Hank Fraley. The decision to sit Mahogany does not happen without his approval. The struggles of so many offensive linemen under his watch shows a lack of preparation and/or execution for the week. Things settled down for the offensive line in the second half, but you have to wonder if that was more of an adjustment from Drew Petzing than improvement from the offensive line. A performance like this is simply inexcusable going forward. Hopefully the same can be said about whatever Mahogany did to warrant the benching.

Winner: Malcolm Rodriguez, LB

With Jack Campbell’s injury, there was a notable question about how to fill his shoes. Derrick Barnes donned the green dot, but since coverage is not his forte, the Lions needed another linebacker to help man the middle. That wound up being Rodriguez, his first true starting assignment since Week 18 of last season. Whereas Rodriguez struggled in 2025 as he returned from his ACL injury, he has turned things around in 2026 in a rotational role. That high level of play continued on Sunday.

Rodriguez was on the field for nearly every defensive snap (55 out of 57) and looked solid in every facet. In run defense, he was stout, registering four run stops per PFF, three of which came in the first half alone. He wound up leading the team in tackles, and he passed the eye test—he was a football-seeking missile. In coverage, he was solid as well, as Miami got minimal production from their running backs and tight ends downfield. He also broke up a pass to Kacmarek in the fourth quarter that should have forced a punt, except the Dolphins got tricky a threw a fake punt of their own.

It was nice to see success over a small sample size translate into a full-game performance for Rodriguez.

Winner: Derrick Moore, DE

The rookie had been a rotational piece early in his career, but with the injury to DJ Wonnum, Moore was presented with a significant opportunity. Rookies Blake Miller, Skyler Gill-Howard, Keith Abney, and Jimmy Rolder (before his injury) each had their moments in the spotlight this season, but Moore had yet to receive his moment in the spotlight. That changed against Miami.

Moore’s outing was not as dominant as Hutchinson’s, but he provided some much-needed pressure off the edge. The impressive part of his game was his hustle, evident on his first-career sack:

Derrick Moore with a third-down sack 😤 pic.twitter.com/WPB62EpMNS
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

Sure, a healthy Willis likely makes the corner, but you still have to credit Moore for pursuing Willis halfway across the field and not letting the quarterback slip by. Moore would add a second sack late in the fourth quarter to help stall a Dolphins comeback attempt. Encouragingly, Moore looked capable in run defense as well—being able to contribute in both run and pass defense was a big part of Wonnum’s game, so getting this kind of production out of the rookie was nice to see.

Winner: Chuck Clark, S

I have been tough on Clark this season, but he deserves flowers for this performance. The interception was a beauty, jumping a Malik Willis deep shot (without drawing pass interference as well) then weaving his way downfield for a 34-yard return deep into Dolphins territory. Perhaps more encouraging than his interception was his coverage in general. Whereas in previous weeks he looked slow or out of place, he was on the ball often on Sunday. He finished the game with five tackles and a pass defended. Best of all, he avoided being on the wrong side of explosive plays.

Winner: Kelvin Sheppard, DC

I had given Sheppard small praises in recent weeks, but I officially have to give him a full write-up. After a brutal start to the season, Sheppard’s defense is now humming, despite a multitude of injuries at key positions. Over the four games, the Lions have allowed 21 points, 17 points, 15 points, and now 9 points. Sure, the Arizona Cardinals, Minnesota Vikings, and Miami Dolphins are not potent offenses, but neither were the New Orleans Saints in Week 1 and New York Jets in Week 3. All you can do is play your opponent, and Sheppard’s defense is a key reason why Detroit has won four in a row.

During the previous three games, the offense did not exceed 20 points scored. In close games like those, one bad defensive drive can cost you a win. That has not happened over the last month. The pass rush has improved and become more consistent. The secondary is minimizing their miscommunications. The scheme finally looks competent and complementary to their talent.

Loser: Red zone offense

This is more of a nebulous “loser” than a singular person. It falls on Jared Goff, it falls on Drew Petzing, it falls on the weapons, and it falls on the offensive line.

Jake Bates kicked four field goals on the day, only the fifth time in his career he had attempted that many kicks. In three of those five games, Bates had attempted a kick from beyond 50-yards—in those cases, the field goal attempt was a chance to salvage points, not settling for easy ones. Against the Dolphins, however, Bates had kicks of the following distances: 43 yards, 33 yards, 40 yards, and 28 yards. Those short kicks illustrate one thing: the offense was driving downfield but failing to finish.

Gibbs managed to get into the end zone on an 8-yard scamper, but as a whole, Detroit uncharacteristically left a lot of points off the board. It’s difficult to pinpoint why Detroit was struggling so much in that regard. The run game was below their normal standard (28 carries for 102 yards, an average of 3.6 yards per attempt). As mentioned, the offensive line was getting beat too often. Perhaps some of their red zone targets were not getting open—Sam LaPorta and Isaac TeSlaa were held to just five catches for 41 yards across the entire game. Maybe Petzing was simply not dialing up successful plays deep in enemy territory.

All I know is that the Lions cannot afford to settle for field goals this often. Against a better opponent, perhaps the Lions go for it more often, but that is still a position the Lions should not be in.

Quick hits:

Winner: Penei Sewell, OT
On a day where the offensive line was getting rocked, Sewell held strong. Having an asset like him on the offensive line is such a benefit to the offense: rain or shine, you can lean on Sewell.

Winners: Tyleik Williams and Alim McNeill, DTs
These two continue to be a terrific tandem. Williams drew a holding call early in the game, while McNeill added a sack in the fourth quarter.

Loser: Jameson Williams, WR
Williams’ only catch, a 31-yarder, sparked the Lions’ lone touchdown drive, but you’d like to see more from him against an opponent like Miami. His only other target was a tough catch but one he should make often than not.

Winner: Rock Ya-Sin, CB
With D.J. Reed out, Ya-Sin saw a sizeable number of snaps and looked solid while doing so. On initial viewing, nothing stood out as negative from his game. A much-needed rebound after getting benched early in the season.

Loser: Keith Abney, DB
Abney is more of a loser by circumstance than performance. Over Detroit’s previous three games, Abney had been heavily involved in the safety rotation. Against Miami, however, his snap count dropped to just six. With a lot of Brian Branch, Chuck Clark, and at least two linebackers, there was not a lot of room for Abney on the field.

Winner: Jack Fox, P
He might throw a better spiral than any quarterback on the Minnesota Vikings roster.

Winner: Dan Campbell, HC
Statistically, it was a below-average game from the Lions, but given the lead up to the week, you have to credit Campbell for being a leader and keeping the team grounded and motivated.

lions.headline: Dan Campbell explains decision to bench Christian Mahogany, start Miles Frazier
lions.body:
Detroit Lions guard Christian Mahogany (73) walks of the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Tuesday, July 22, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions made a very surprising personnel decision in their 19-9 win over the Miami Dolphins. Lions coach Dan Campbell decided to give Miles Frazier his first career start at left guard over Christian Mahogany. There weren’t any indications that Mahogany’s play had dipped—in fact, he was nationally praised for his performance against the Vikings—so his benching came as a complete surprise.

After the Lions’ win, Campbell explained the decision, noting it was a disciplinary action.

“That was team rules (for) Mahogany. It was really that simple,” Campbell said. “Miles deserved his opportunity, so he got it. Doesn’t mean it stays that way, but that was the way it was going to be today.”

In his first career start, Frazier clearly struggled in the first half, giving up several early pressures to Dolphins defensive tackle Zach Sieler. He did settle down in the second half, though, helping the Lions score on every second-half possession—outside of the last drive that bled the remainder of the clock.

Still, there will be plenty of questions going forward about what exactly Mahogany did to earn a benching. Not only was he getting national praise and passing the eye test, but he has earned PFF’s 10th-highest grade among guards with at least 130 snaps.

Hopefully, he can get back in the Lions’ good graces and continue his strong season.

UPDATE: According to Lions beat reporter Justin Rogers, Mahogany exited the locker room as soon as media showed up, so we have no clarification on what rule he broke.

lions.headline: 5 takeaways from Detroit Lions’ 19-9 win against Miami Dolphins
lions.body:
MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 08: Derrick Moore #8 of the Detroit Lions rushes Malik Willis #2 of the Miami Dolphins during the first half of the game at Hard Rock Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Entering Week 9 on a three-game winning streak, the Detroit Lions flew down south to face the Miami Dolphins. The Lions offense was expected to have a big game, but was held to just 19 points against a Dolphins defense that gave them fits. Those 19 points were enough in the end as Detroit’s defense held Miami to just nine points.

Here are my five takeaways from the Lions’ victory against the Dolphins.

Miles Frazier gets his first career start

The biggest storyline was left guard Christian Mahogany not getting the start. He did play on special teams, so it wasn’t an injury. The CBS broadcast said the reason was a “coaching decision.” With him not getting the start, the team called on backup guard Miles Frazier to play left guard.

After the game, Lions head coach Dan Campbell was asked about this and explained why Frazier got the start.

“That was team rules (for) Mahogany. It was really that simple,” Campbell said. “Miles deserved his opportunity, so he got it. Doesn’t mean it stays that way, but that was the way it was going to be today.”

Hopefully Mahogany can get back on the team’s good side, or else he could cost himself not just a job, but a possible contract extension in the future.

Offensive line struggled

Detroit’s offensive line struggled against a struggling Miami defense. Frazier was a big part of the problem, missing blocks repeatedly and struggling to hold his blocks, but he wasn’t the only culprit. Right tackle Blake Miller had his worst game of the season, allowing tons of pressure and looking like a rookie.

Lions quarterback Jared Goff was sacked three times, and he threw his second interception of the season when Dolphins EDGE Josh Uche hit him as he threw. Goff was also hit as he threw another pass that was initially ruled a fumble recovered by the Dolphins for a touchdown, but it was overturned to an incomplete pass. Goff faced pressure for most of the game, and it hurt the offense.

In the running game, running back Jahmyr Gibbs was limited in his lanes, rushing 20 times for 74 yards and was the only player to find the end zone. We have seen what this team looks like when the offensive line struggles—look back at the 2025 season. Hopefully Mahogany and backup center Cade Mays can return for the trip to Germany next week, as performances like this won’t win you many games.

The calls for firing Kelvin Sheppard have quieted down

After a long September where the Lions’ defense was a liability, it has become an asset in their last four games. They allowed 21 points against the Arizona Cardinals, but held the Green Bay Packers, Minnesota Vikings, and Miami Dolphins to 16, 15, and nine points respectively. This defense is creating turnovers, generating pressure, and stopping the running game.

Remember when fans were clamoring for Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard to be fired? This team was also without starting EDGE DJ Wonnum, cornerback D.J. Reed, and linebacker Jack Campbell. The good news is Wonnum and Reed should be back soon, and safety Kerby Joseph is getting closer to returning. With the play improving and players returning from injury soon, this defense is starting to turn a corner.

Down multiple starters, the defense performed well overall, holding Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon II to 55 yards, just 3.4 yards per carry. Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis faced pressure for most of the game, getting sacked three times as rookie EDGE Derrick Moore picked up the first and second sacks of his NFL career.

Derrick Moore with a third-down sack 😤 pic.twitter.com/WPB62EpMNS
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

When Willis had time to throw, he didn’t look that good. He had some nice plays removed because of the offense’s lack of discipline, but he was held to 128 passing yards and seven rushing yards. Lions safety Chuck Clark also picked him off, his second of the year.

Miami’s penalties helped Detroit in a big way

While the Lions defense played well, they got bailed out a few times by the Dolphins’ own mistakes. Whether it was a false start, offensive pass interference, or holding, the Dolphins kept shooting themselves in the foot. Willis had a great 50+ yard throw overturned for holding, and a few successful runs by Gordon were wiped away as well. If Detroit couldn’t stop them, the Dolphins stopped themselves.

If Miami didn’t get called for as many flags as they did, this game could’ve been a lot closer, or possibly Miami could’ve won this game. It’s hard to win football games when you are beating yourself, and that is what Miami did, getting  11 penalties for 87 yards.

Shoutout Jake Bates

On offense, the Lions leaned on kicker Jake Bates. Bates made all four field goal attempts, the longest from 43 yards. He did make a mistake on kickoff where he didn’t land it in the landing zone, but besides that, he was the best player for the Lions when it came to putting points on the board. It helps having a kicker you can rely on to put up points and make drives worthwhile when the offense can’t find the end zone.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Dolphins recap, highlights: Detroit’s defense dominates in 19-9 win
lions.body:
Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard arrives in linebacker Jack Campbell’s jersey ahead of the game against Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions offense has failed to score more than 20 points in three straight weeks, but the defense has carried them to wins in all three of those games.

It was the same story in the Lions’ Week 9 win over the Miami Dolphins. The offense was disjointed and had to overcome some poor offensive line play early. And while they eventually were able to find some success late, Detroit’s defensive performance is what really stood out.

The Lions held the Dolphins to just 77 yards rushing and 3.7 yards per carry. Miami quarterback Malik Willis had just 128 passing yards. And, most importantly, the Lions held the Dolphins out of the end zone completely for all four quarters.

It was an inspired performance, particularly without the heartbeat of the defense, Jack Campbell. The Lions clearly dedicated the game to him, sporting No. 46 jerseys while walking into the stadium. And while Campbell vowed this week to eventually continue his NFL career, Detroit proved on Sunday that they can operate without him for now.

Here’s a full recap of the Lions’ 19-9 win over the Dolphins.

First quarter

The Lions got the ball first and had great field position after the kickoff landed before the landing zone. Interestingly, it was Miles Frazier at left guard to start the game in place of the (presumably) healthy Christian Mahogany. After picking up 6 yards on the first two plays, Jared Goff and the Lions faced an quick third-and-4. Goff found Amon-Ra St. Brown for a nice gain of 16 yards between Dolphins’ zone coverage defenders. Detroit failed to pick up the next third-and-short when Goff’s arm was hit by Dolphins defender Josh Uche.

That set up a fourth-and-3 from the Dolphins’ 31-yard line. Detroit went for it, and Goff avoided pressure to find Isaac TeSlaa for 8 to keep the drive alive. Then Jahmyr Gibbs took a wildcat snap, faked a pitch to Goff, and took it for 16 yards down to the Dolphins’ 6-yard line.

Little wildcat action pic.twitter.com/oEdr5UP3Ni
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

But on third-and-goal, Goff was sacked by Uche, forcing the Lions to settled for a chip-shot field goal. 3-0 Lions.

Detroit managed to get a quick three-and-out on defense after two rushes went for 0 yards, and Malik Willis’ third-down pass was too far for his receiver.

But the Lions quickly gave the ball back to Miami. After two successful runs, Goff’s arm was hit again by Uche while throwing, and the ball went right to Dolphins defensive back Chris Johnson.

Dolphins rookie Chris Johnson picks off Goff!

DETvsMIA on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/p3fgZMJ66F
— NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026

Miami moved into scoring position with a leaping grab from Caleb Douglas for 20 yards down to the Lions’ 20-yard line. In the red zone, the Dolphins faced a third-and-11 and they tried to catch Detroit sleeping with a draw play. But Aidan Hutchinson sniffed it out for a short gain, and the Dolphins settled for a field goal to tie it up. 3-3 tie.

The Lions offense gained just 3 yards on their first two plays to set up a big third-and-7 to start the second quarter.

Second quarter

On the first play, Goff went deep to Jameson Williams, but the receiver bobbled a very catchable ball and the Lions were forced to punt…. or were they?!? Jack Fox drilled a pass to Tay Martin for the fake punt conversion and 11 yards.

What a throw, @MrJackFox pic.twitter.com/n3m4I5phod
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

Detroit had to dig themselves out of hole, though, as Frazier was called for a holding penalty on the next play. While an 11-yard pass to St. Brown helped, a failed screen set up a third-and-9. And on the play, the Dolphins sent an aggressive blitz and Miami picked up their third sack of the game. This time, the Lions did actually punt the ball away.

The Dolphins were pinned at their own 5-yard line, but a play-action pass to Greg Dulcich for 11 yards got Miami out of the jam. That said, Hutchinson drew a holding penalty that eventually set up a third-and-18 for the Dolphins. Pressure from the Lions forced Willis to throw it away.

Despite a holding penalty on the Lions on the punt, they still got great field position due to a shank from Dolphins punter Bradley Pinion. Detroit started on their own 43-yard line, hoping to put some of the offensive line issues behind them. The drive started promisingly with an 11-yard pass to Sam LaPorta and a 10-yard run from Gibbs. Two plays later, Goff hit St. Brown for another 14 yards.

However, the drive stalled from there. A toss to Gibbs lost 3 yards. Then another Gibbs run lost another 3 yards. Goff scrambled on third down to make the field goal a little shorter, and Bates drilled a 40-yard field goal to make it 6-3 Lions with 3:30 left in the half.

Miami responded before the half ended. A reverse to Kevin Coleman earned 16 yards and put the Dolphins in Lions territory. Ollie Gordon then got Miami into field goal range with a pair of draws that went for 9 and 11 yards. Eventually, Miami drove down to the Lions’ 10-yard line and had a shot at the end zone. But Hutchinson drew another holding penalty, forcing the Dolphins to kick a game-tying field goal, but former Lions Zane Gonzalez missed a 38-yard field goal to keep it 6-3 Lions at halftime.

Third quarter

Miami started with the ball and picked up a quick first down thanks to a pass interference penalty on Derrick Barnes. He made amends with a tackle for loss on the next play, helping set up a third-and-11 for the Dolphins. Willis tried to force a ball into a tight window, but safety Chuck Clark picked it off and returned it all the way to the Dolphins 26-yard line.

Chuck Clark picked it off! pic.twitter.com/I98vZOuzbq
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

Gibbs gave the Lions a new set of downs inside the red zone with a third-and-1 conversion with a 3-yard gain on a toss. However, the Lions had to settle for another field goal when a second down Gibbs run went for no gain and Sam LaPorta committed a false start to set up a third-and-11. Goff turfed a pass to Gibbs, and Bates was good from 33. 9-3 Lions.

Bates’ ensuing kickoff was well short of the landing zone, setting the Dolphins up at the 40-yard line. Miami turned that into points. One key play was a third-and-11 pass to Douglas, who ran a 9-yard curl, then avoided a tackle attempt from Ennis Rakestraw to get the first down. Detroit drew another holding penalty—Skyler Gill-Howard this time. And it forced Miami to settle for another field goal attempt. This time Gonzalez was good from 52 yards. 9-6 Lions.

Detroit looked to retaliate quickly. A 31-yard strike to Jameson Williams immediately put the Lions in field goal position on the first play of the drive.

31 yards to Jamo to start the drive! pic.twitter.com/3VHq05KCZ6
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

Goff hit St. Brown for 17 on the very next play, putting Detroit into the red zone. The Lions then faced a third-and-1, and the Dolphins were all over Detroit’s play-action attempt. The Lions obviously went for it on fourth-and-1, and Detroit dialed up a well-timed pitch to Gibbs, who beat everyone to the outside for an 8-yard touchdown. 16-6 Lions.

Gibbs takes the fourth-down toss for six! pic.twitter.com/0mNX8r98Qg
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

Miami faced a third-and-3 at the start of the fourth quarter.

Fourth quarter

The Dolphins failed to convert after Malcolm Rodriguez punched out the ball on what would’ve been a converted first down pass. But Miami pulled off a fake punt of their own, and it was even more successful than Detroit’s, gaining 46 yards.

Dolphins draw up a fake punt of their own! That's two fake punts this game.

DETvsMIA on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/caEvejdds1
— NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026

Then, on a third-and-5 inside the red zone, Willis found Malik Washington for 7 yards to move the chain. Alim McNeill tallied a sack to put the Dolphins in a tough third-and-goal situation from the 13.

Alim with the sack! pic.twitter.com/52nHxtN1q3
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

Derrick Moore chased down Willis on third down, forcing yet another field goal from the Dolphins. 16-9 Lions.

Detroit avoided a third-and-out when an attempt to St. Brown drew a 17-yard pass interference penalty. That would be all the Lions could muster, though. A holding penalty on Blake Miller pushed the Lions back, but Detroit dug out of it with a 17-yard screen to St. Brown on a third-and-8.

Amon-Ra moving the chains with a 17-yard pickup on third down pic.twitter.com/IFjcA5x5Hb
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

Detroit would stall out from there, as Goff overthrew St. Brown on third-and-7. Bates’ 43-yard field goal was good, to give Detroit a two-score lead with 4:28 left. 19-9 Lions.

Starting at their own 35-yard line, the Dolphins had to score twice and score quickly. But Detroit’s defensive line took over. Hutchinson forced a throw away on first down, Moore got a sack on second down, and on fourth-and-12, the Dolphins dropped a potential conversion. Detroit took over at Miami’s 33 with 3:02 left and the game in hand.

Derrick Moore gets another one 😤 pic.twitter.com/O8Pt7Zpf7n
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

The Lions offense managed to earn a couple of first downs and bleed the rest of the clock to move to 6-2 on the season at the midway point of the year.

lions.headline: Report: Lions LB Jack Campbell determined to play football again
lions.body:
Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell (46) before OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, June 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

According to the CBS NFL pregame show, Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell remains hospitalized with the neck injury he suffered last Sunday against the Minnesota Vikings. Sideline reporter Melanie Collins added another bit of interesting information, noting that Campbell—in her words—“he is determined to get back on this football.” Per Collins, Campbell told Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell:

“Just make sure the house is taken care of until I can get back.”

The last definitive update we’ve gotten from Jack Campbell was a written statement through the Lions in which Campbell said, “I have full movement in my lower body, and I’m continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body. I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic. I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”

Since then, Dan Campbell has said the Lions linebacker continues to get better. And on Sunday, several Lions players and coaches showed up to their Week 9 game against the Miami Dolphins donning Campbell’s jerseys.

For 4️⃣6️⃣ pic.twitter.com/43xSI718tJ
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

On Saturday, the Lions placed Campbell on injured reserve, meaning he’ll miss at least the next four games. It’s still unclear if his 2026 season is over, but it appears Campbell doesn’t believe his NFL career is over.

"He is determined to get back on this football field, telling Dan Campbell: 'Just make sure the house is taken care of until I can get back.'"@Melanie_Collins with an update on @Lions' hospitalized linebacker Jack Campbell pic.twitter.com/evtukOE2S0
— NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) November 8, 2026

As always, if any updates are given on Campbell’s status or the future of his NFL career, we’ll continue to provide updates here at PrideOfDetroit.com. In the meantime, continue to send your best hopes and wishes to the Campbell family.

The Detroit Lions are coming off back-to-back intense NFC North rivalry games and now head south to take on the struggling Miami Dolphins. Detroit enters the game on a three-game winning streak and looks to keep it alive before heading to Germany.

Last week, my predictions went one-for-three, with the Lions’ defense holding up their end of the bargain, but the offense wasn’t as explosive. Quarterback Jared Goff couldn’t throw as much as I wanted, and wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown was limited as running back Jahmyr Gibbs took over the game in the second half.

With us back at even, it’s time to get back on the winning side on Sunday. The odds are with FanDuel Sportsbook.

1. Jahmyr Gibbs 125+ rushing yards (+220)

Speaking of Gibbs, he should continue that hot streak heading into Week 9. The Dolphins’ run defense has been rough, ranked 31st in PFF with a 51 run-defense grade and 26th in DVOA against the run. While they’re allowing only 113 rushing yards per game, this offensive line could be the best unit they’ve faced this season. How the Lions offense finished the game against the Vikings last week, where they ran it down their throats, felt like a moment when everything clicked on the offensive line.

Miami has faced top-end running back talent this season in Christian McCaffrey and Kenneth Walker III, but Gibbs has turned his game up during the winning streak. He’s averaging 140 yards per game, and that’s up against one of the best defenses in the Vikings and a solid defense in the Green Bay Packers. Facing a defense that is struggling to stop the run, I think Gibbs has another stellar performance on Sunday.

Bet potential winnings: $10 -> $32

2. Malik Willis under 208.5 passing yards (-113)

Back-to-back matchups against struggling offenses, I think Detroit can take care of business defensively. Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis is averaging 181 passing yards a game, and despite the Lions being without cornerback D.J. Reed, this secondary has been improving during this win streak. The Dolphins’ passing attack also lacks playmakers, which should make it easier for the Detroit defense to defend.

The Lions secondary held the Vikings with a fully healthy offense of Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, T.J. Hockenson, and Kyler Murray to just 185 passing yards. Now, they face a team with Malik Washington and Greg Dulcich as their top options. No disrespect, but those players are not on the same level as the Vikings’ receiving core.

The Dolphins’ poor offensive line play will also help. Ranked 31st in pass blocking with a 53.6 PFF grade, going up against a Lions pass rush ranked third (79.9 grade) in PFF, Willis could have a long day in the pocket. He can move his legs to extend plays, but he might have to do that all game against Lions EDGE Aidan Hutchinson. I can’t see Willis having a dominant game against an improving defense that will play their hearts out for their star linebacker, Jack Campbell.

Covering tight ends has been a problem for the Dolphins defense. Through seven games, they’ve allowed 483 yards and six touchdowns by tight ends. The Lions’ passing offense could be searching for answers if St. Brown has a limited snap count due to his injury, which opens the door for a touchdown for tight end Sam LaPorta.

LaPorta had a hot start to the season, scoring three touchdowns and getting 40+ yards per game in the first five games. michigan.headline: The State Of Our Open Threads - After Michigan State
michigan.body:
The State Of Our Open Threads - After Michigan State

I am going to be honest with everyone here.
From the middle of the third quarter onwards, I was basically watching last night's game with a sort of resigned detachment. I was watching a very good defense yet again being wasted by a functionally non-existent offense. I found myself thinking about what this game would look like if we simply had mere competency on that side of the ball, if we would do what, say, MSU was doing and just run a basic, nondescript offense that...works.
What scares me is that this is probably as talented a team as Whittingham, for as long as he is here, will have. Attrition is a big thing now, and you get the sense that Kyle on the recruiting trail, if he has even bothered with that, lands as flat as anyone without a proper parachute. It has been a long time since I have earnestly walked away from a TV, or walked out of a stadium, saying, "Jesus, this sucks."
And what I find comforting to know is that many of you feel as I do.
Let's talk about this.
There were 3049 posts in the open thread when the game mercifully ended, and there were 1,708 instances of tracked words, which came to an efficiency rating of 1.79, which for as long as I've done this - since Hoke - is comfortably in loss territory. It took a decade, but we're close to this being a predictive tool now. I know, you're thrilled - it was the only happy moment I had last night. Below is the season trend:

Losses always significantly affect the number of fucks we give. For the entire run of this, across a couple staffs now, there is something like a 130-150 fuck difference on average between a win and a loss, and when you look at 398 fucks given last night in contrast to the 235 we gave for Rutgers, that more or less holds.
It's less with "shits" since we never give nearly as many, but there is still a reasonably constant variation of about 30-40 between wins and losses, and indeed, we gave 162 shits last night, up 32 from the Rutgers game. There are always outliers, but the pattern has been fairly constant now even accounting for staff changes.

We need to discuss this one a bit, because clearly we've made our decision. It was true until the Penn State game that "fire" and "suck" trended together, which is actually reasonably normal for this study. However, like the end of Hoke's time here, there was a game where we made a decision as a blog and "fire" jumped significantly. In 2014, it was Minnesota. Here, it was Indiana, but as you can see, last night didn't help matters. Indeed, we more than doubled "fire" - 291 last night, 122 last week.

An example of a drill-down comparison here - this is the number of times "fire" is mentioned compared to the number of times someone types "Whittingham" or "Whitt". Not the strongest correlation, I know, but they correlate enough that you can see the object of rage coming into focus. It would be a similar story for Jason Beck too, of course.

There is always this too. Again, in most seasons, these haven't had much to do with one another, but this years, well, the record does speak for itself. When you can't find the end zone against a hobbled 2-6 team, even with your own OL problems, then....well....what else is there but "suck"?

This one is becoming interesting too. We talk about the "Defense" and "Offense" more or less equally, but in vastly different contexts, as you will note from some of the data and comments about. The defense does its job, whereas the offense is there to utterly job the defense by being able to do nothing.

This is the normalized value chart for conference play. It hasn't been a good season, and it became objectively worse last night.

We get Oregon next, folks, and Oregon beat Ohio State rather convincingly. I wonder if Oregon would let us borrow their second string on offense, which is likely better than our first.

michigan.headline: Jason Beck Fired, Harding Interim OC
michigan.body:
Jason Beck Fired, Harding Interim OC

Seth
November 8th, 2026 at 8:28 PM

As you probably have heard, offensive coordinator Jason Beck was terminated today, with offensive line coach Jim Harding named interim coordinator.
“The results have not matched our desired outcome, and I felt that a change in leadership was required for our offense,” said Whittingham. “We need to put our offensive players and the entire team in the best possible position to be successful.

Whittingham told the press early this morning he would "evaluate everything after the season." Apparently someone since then convinced the Tsar this couldn't wait.
It's a little late to be calling bad boyars, however. Both Sam Webb and Chris Balas referenced insiders who said the offensive structure was broken in fall practice, and it was clear after the opener that Beck was in over his head. The fanbase quickly seized on the most visible of his faults—the eccentric, situationally nonsensical "Rhino" position, a tendency to tip his snap timing, and the many promising drives that prematurely stalled because the man was unquestionably the worst short yardage playcaller in the game's history. Coaches and people who chart things found more damning evidence, from nonsensical "eye-candy" motions that wasted plays and practice time, to a total inability to install a base and iterate from it. Most damningly, Beck was handed almost all of a top-25 running game, plus JJ Buchanan and a ten-year reputation as the school that runs the damn ball, and irreparably dismantled it in the span of one offseason.
Had this announcement come after the Iowa, Minnesota, or Indiana debacles, this fanbase probably would have believed Beck an unfortunate but understandable mistake. Instead, it looks like Whittingham had to be forced into a decision after dragging the program to its lowest point since the season Georgia Tech asked if we'd sit our Black player and we went "Sure!"
The offense is far too broken to expect any meaningful improvement this year. Even if they could bring in a new coach and install his stuff by year's end, Michigan would have to win at Oregon, at home versus undefeated UCLA, or at Ohio State to even earn those bowl practices. Neither does removing Beck solve the mounting injuries, Underwood's benching-worthy regression, Carr's unreadiness, and repeated miscues up and down the roster, most notably among Harding's linemen.
But the program-wide disorganization, arbitrary accountability, and the fact things had to get this bad before any of it was addressed does fall on one pair of shoulders. Jason Beck is not the reason the nation's highest paid coordinator and highest paid sophomore quarterback are writeoffs this moment. I doubt there's more than a handful of Michigan fans right now who don't want to see Whittingham fired. The top two reasons not to do so this minute are his buyout would drop to a more manageable $25 million at season's end, and the absentee AD who hired him has himself already been given a $7.14 million severance to step down at the end of the year.
[After THE JUMP: A really cute bear cub. How sweet.]

Told ya! [Patrick Barron]

michigan.headline: Kyle Whittingham explains why he fired Michigan Football OC Jason Beck
michigan.body:
Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham walks up the tunnel after 13-6 loss to Indiana in overtime at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Michigan has made a major change to its coaching staff in the middle of a tough season, as head coach Kyle Whittingham announced on Sunday evening that he was firing offensive coordinator Jason Beck.

In a statement released by the program, Whittingham explained why he made the decision:

“The results have not matched our desired outcome, and I felt that a change in leadership was required for our offense,” Whittingham said. “We need to put our offensive players and the entire team in the best possible position to be successful.

“We appreciate the hard work and effort that Jason has dedicated to the program. Jason is a great man and coach, and unfortunately, it did not work out the way that we wanted it to at Michigan. We wish Jason and his family nothing but the best in the future.”

Offensive line coach Jim Harding will serve as interim offensive coordinator for the rest of the season, and Whittingham will conduct a national search for the next offensive coordinator for the Wolverines.

The firing comes one day after Michigan’s 15-6 brutal loss to Michigan State, its first loss to the Spartans since 2021. The Wolverines finished with a season-low 192 total yards, turned the ball over four times and went 2-of-10 on third down. Freshman quarterback Tommy Carr was also sacked five times, while the run game averaged 2.1 yards per carry on 26 attempts. The pass game produced just 138 yards.

After the game, Whittingham said the team took “three steps back” and that he was “as disappointed and frustrated as I’ve ever been as a head coach.” He also acknowledged “some serious issues” and said the loss “falls on me.”

Michigan’s offense has struggled all season. Before Saturday, it ranked among the bottom of the country in yards per game, and the passing attack was one of the least productive nationally. Now after the game, those offensive stats are:

Total offense: No. 132 (out of 138)

Scoring offense: No. 126

Rushing offense: No. 109

Passing offense: No. 125

Total number of first downs: No. 124

Red zone offense: No. 129

The Wolverines also made a quarterback change in the middle of the season, replacing Bryce Underwood with freshman Tommy Carr at halftime against Penn State. That move paid off in that game, but the offense has still be flat since then, for the most part.

Whittingham has said he is confident the program will be fixed. “I promise you, we’ll eventually get this thing right,” he said after the Michigan State game on Saturday. Firing his own offensive coordinator who he brought with him from Utah is the first major step in that effort.

michigan.headline: Michigan Football fires offensive coordinator Jason Beck
michigan.body:
Michigan offensive coordinator Jason Beck looks on before the spring game at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, April 18, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Not even 24 hours following the Wolverines’ embarrassing 15-6 loss to Michigan State at The Big House in which they only compiled 192 total yards, went 2-of-10 on third down and only scored a touchdown in garbage time against one of the worst defenses in all of college football, the Michigan football program is moving in a new direction offensively.

Per multiple reports and later confirmed by the program, Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham has fired offensive coordinator Jason Beck.

Michigan has struggled consistently on offense all season long. The Wolverines rank near the bottom in nearly every offensive category across the FBS, including:

Total offense: No. 132 (out of 138)

Scoring offense: No. 126

Rushing offense: No. 109

Passing offense: No. 125

Total number of first downs: No. 124

Red zone offense: No. 129

Beck was one of Whittingham’s first hires at Michigan, with Beck coming over from Utah. The Utes’ were ranked No. 6 nationally in 2025 by averaging 478.6 yards per game, second in rushing offense with 269.8 rushing yards per game and 37 rushing touchdowns, and No. 5 in scoring offense, averaging 41.1 points per game. All that — combined with all the talent on the roster — makes Michigan’s lack of success on offense all that more baffling.

“Well, last year, Jason was exceptional. And we had exceptional results. And so I’m not going to say that he’s struggling,” Whittingham said after the Indiana loss, showing faith in a coach that Michigan’s fanbase has lost belief in.

Given Beck’s success calling plays at Utah and his previous success at New Mexico (the Lobos ranked No. 5 in the FBS in rushing offense in 2024, averaging 253.6 yards per game), Michigan fans were excited for Beck to come in get the most of Bryce Underwood and a young Michigan offense. That excitement has turned into fury in less than two months, with Beck leading a Michigan offense that is among the worst in all of college football.

It’s unclear where Michigan goes from here. Aside from Hill, the rest of this coaching staff still needs to prove they are worth keeping around next season, Whittingham included.

Stay with Maize n Brew for what’s next. There’s never a dull moment when it comes to Michigan football.

Michigan’s disappointing football season took another turn for the worse Saturday night, as the Wolverines fell to Michigan State at The Big House to surrender the Paul Bunyan Trophy for the first time since 2021.

Despite holding the Spartans without a touchdown, Michigan couldn’t get anything going offensively. The Wolverines committed four turnovers, surrendered five sacks and failed to find the end zone until the final two minutes of regulation. Quarterback Tommy Carr struggled to replicate his success at Rutgers, while Michigan’s offense as a whole managed just 54 official rushing yards.

The defense kept Michigan within striking distance throughout the night, but the Spartans controlled the clock for more than 38 minutes and gradually pulled away behind five field goals.

Here’s a closer look at how the Wolverines performed, according to Pro Football Focus.

Offensive team grades

Jason Beck’s offense took a significant step backward Saturday night, earning a 55.9 overall after posting a 78.8 against Rutgers the previous week.
